---
title: "P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction"
---

## The question

A seed can remain dormant in apparently suitable soil. A shoot bends towards
light, and a mature plant begins flowering after the season changes. Explain
how perception, signalling, altered cellular activity and organ development
connect. Distinguish a response from proof of its underlying mechanism.

## From stimulus to response

A signal must be detected by an appropriate receptor. Detection changes
downstream activity, which can modify existing proteins, transport, metabolism
or gene expression. The response depends on tissue, developmental state and
other signals. A receptor is not the final response itself, and the amount of
a hormone is not the only determinant of sensitivity.

Gene expression connects a shared genome to specialised behaviour. Transcription
produces RNA; some RNAs support protein synthesis and others act directly.
Regulatory proteins can change which genes are used and when. Changing gene
expression does not require changing DNA sequence. Fast ion-channel responses
can precede slower changes in organ anatomy.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  cue[Environmental or internal cue] --> receptor[Perception]
  receptor --> fast[Existing protein and transport activity]
  receptor --> expr[Gene-expression changes]
  fast --> cell[Cell physiology]
  expr --> cell
  cell --> organ[Growth or developmental response]
  state[Tissue and developmental state] --> cell
```

This original scheme is a reasoning framework. Actual pathways have feedback,
interactions and distinct timescales. Use it to locate the evidence: does an
experiment measure a stimulus, an intermediate or the final phenotype?

## Hormones operate in interacting networks

Plant hormones are signalling molecules active at low concentrations. Their
effects depend on production, transport, metabolism and perception. One hormone
can affect several processes, and several hormones can affect one process.
The following are useful entry points rather than one-to-one rules:

| Signal class | Useful example | Interpretation caution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Auxin | Directional growth, root initiation and developmental patterning | Concentration, transport and tissue sensitivity matter |
| Cytokinins | Cell division, meristem activity and resource-related responses | Effects interact with other signals and developmental state |
| Gibberellins | Germination and stem elongation in appropriate contexts | Not every dwarf plant lacks gibberellin |
| ABA | Dormancy and water-stress responses | ABA responses include both rapid physiology and longer-term development |
| Ethylene | Fruit ripening in responsive species and other developmental/stress responses | Not all fruits use identical ripening regulation |
| Brassinosteroids | Growth and differentiation | Effects depend on interaction with other pathways |
| Jasmonates and salicylic acid | Defence and associated growth changes | Different attackers and conditions recruit different combinations |

Memorising this table is insufficient. Explain a case as signal → cellular
process → organ consequence. For example, a change in auxin distribution can
produce unequal expansion across an organ. Root and shoot growth responses
to the same auxin change can differ. “Auxin promotes growth” hides this
important context dependence.

## Light supplies information as well as energy

Photoreceptors allow plants to detect spectral composition, direction and
timing. Phytochromes respond to red/far-red light, while blue-light receptors
include cryptochromes and phototropins. These signals influence developmental
choices beyond photosynthetic energy supply. A seedling can change form after
a small informative light exposure without obtaining much fixed carbon from it.

Red/far-red balance can provide information about neighbouring vegetation.
A shoot may respond with altered elongation and resource allocation. This
can improve access to light but can also increase vulnerability or reduce
investment elsewhere. A response is conditional, not evidence that plants
predict an intentional goal.

Phototropism involves directional light perception and differential growth.
Gravitropism involves gravity perception, signal redistribution and asymmetric
responses. Gravitational orientation and light direction are different cues;
an experimental design must separate them before assigning a mechanism.
Rotating a pot changes several physical relationships and requires controls.

## Germination depends on state and conditions

Imbibition restores hydration, and metabolism resumes as conditions permit.
Reserve mobilisation supports the developing seedling. Radicle emergence is
a commonly used operational measure of germination, but later establishment
requires further growth and resource acquisition.

**Dormancy** means a viable seed does not germinate despite otherwise suitable
conditions. **Quiescence** reflects unsuitable external conditions such as
insufficient water. Dormancy can involve embryo state, surrounding tissues and
signal balance. ABA and gibberellin pathways provide a useful model of
interacting regulation, but species differ in requirements for temperature,
light or other cues.

A germination percentage needs a clear denominator and time. Twelve germinated
seeds out of twenty by day five gives 60%, not proof that eight are dead.
They could germinate later, be dormant, or be non-viable. Independent dishes
or pots matter when environmental treatment is shared. Twenty seeds in one
dish do not automatically give twenty independent temperature treatments.

## Vegetative growth combines production and allocation

Meristems generate organs while expansion changes their dimensions. Hormones,
nutrients, carbon status and environment coordinate these processes. Apical
dominance illustrates integration: shoot-tip activity influences lateral bud
outgrowth through several interacting signals and resource relations. Removing
an apex changes more than one hormone concentration and creates a wound.
An altered branching pattern alone cannot identify the complete mechanism.

Secondary growth increases girth through lateral meristems. Cambial activity
must be coordinated with transport and support as the shoot enlarges. Seasonal
activity can alter xylem properties. A ring or tissue pattern records growth,
but interpreting it requires knowledge of species and environmental history.

## Flowering connects leaves and the shoot apex

Plants integrate age, resource status, temperature and light timing. Photoperiod
responses depend on the species and can involve the duration of the night as
well as the day. Vernalisation refers to promotion of flowering competence by
extended cold in responsive plants. It is different from a universal direct
trigger that makes every cold-treated plant flower immediately.

In Arabidopsis, FT provides an example of a mobile signal linking leaves with
the shoot apex. Experiments expressing tagged FT and using grafts supported
protein movement contributing to floral induction. This is evidence for a
particular mechanism in a model system, not proof that all flowering control
is identical. See the primary study by
[Corbesier and colleagues](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17446353/).

At the apex, altered gene activity changes meristem identity and organ
development. Flower induction, formation of floral organs, gametophyte
development, pollination, fertilisation and fruit development are distinct
steps. Failure at one step need not mean that flowering was not induced.

## Reproduction links generations

In flowering plants, pollen delivers sperm cells to the female gametophyte.
Double fertilisation produces a zygote and endosperm, with the latter supporting
seed development in an appropriate species-specific pattern. Embryogenesis
establishes the next plant's body organisation. Fruit derives from maternal
tissue and can assist protection and dispersal; a seed and a fruit are not
equivalent structures.

Developing seeds and fruits draw resources as sinks. Carbon limitation, water
stress or temperature can affect reproductive success after a normal-looking
flower forms. Measure seed number, viability or yield separately from flower
number when those are the actual biological goals.

## Senescence can redistribute resources

Senescence is a regulated developmental process that can mobilise nutrients
from ageing tissues. Programmed cell death participates in development and
defence, but it should not be treated as synonymous with every senescence
stage or every form of accidental injury. A yellowing leaf may reflect normal
ageing, deficiency, stress or several processes. Tissue age and environmental
controls are needed to distinguish explanations.

[OpenStax plant sensory systems](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/30-6-plant-sensory-systems-and-responses).
